title: Steady-state entanglement harvesting for two rotating atoms in a cylindrical cavity
authors: Hong-Tao Zheng, Xiang-Fa Zhou, Guang-Can Guo and Zheng-Wei Zhou
abstract: We study the entanglement dynamics of two rotating atoms (with two internal levels and ) in a cylindrical cavity, which interact with a massless scalar field in vacuum satisfying the Dirichlet boundary condition. Our analysis demonstrates that it is possible to obtain the steady-state entanglement under two types of resonant conditions. For two identical atoms with the same world-line, the system reduces to the usual dissipative Dicke model at the first resonant condition where and are the energy splitting and the angular velocity of the th atom, and is the Lorentz factor. The entangled steady-state takes the form where and are constant, which is consistent with the previous study (see 2022 Phys. Rev. D 106 105028). For two atoms with different world-lines, the system suffers from a significant mixed joint dissipation process at the second resonant condition , and reaches an entangled steady-state as . Moreover, with the help of the cavity, we can obtain a much higher concurrence in the final states by changing the relative ratio of the two orbital radii. Our work thus provides a more effective way for the extraction of steady-state entanglement from the vacuum via the analogue Unruh effect for two rotating atoms in a cylindrical cavity.

title: Observation of alignment tensor effects in metastability-exchange collisions with highly polarized 3 ...
authors: Yida Sha, Kaiwen Yi, Xingqing Jin, Matteo Fadel and Xiang Peng
abstract: Highly polarized ensembles prepared by metastability-exchange optical pumping (MEOP) have been widely used in precision measurements and fundamental physics. Metastability-exchange (ME) collisions, serving as the basis of MEOP, are traditionally described in terms of atomic orientation, while the significant contributions of metastable alignment tensor at high polarization remain unexplored. In this work, we develop a linearized model under mean-field approximation to investigate alignment tensor effects in highly polarized , which originate from the metastable manifold and are revealed through ME-induced relaxation and frequency shift. By means of free-induction-decay measurements, a pronounced dependence on nuclear polarization is experimentally observed in the response of the ground-state-metastable hybrid ensembles to the external magnetic field. Furthermore, after obtaining the characteristics of tensor-induced phenomena, we demonstrate good agreement between the experiment and the theory. This work advances the understanding of nuclear spin dynamics in highly polarized using MEOP. It further provides applications in systematic error correction of high-accuracy magnetometry, as well as in optimal protocol for the generation of nuclear spin-squeezed states.

title: Distributing graph states with a photon-weaving quantum server
abstract: One of the key aims of quantum networks is the efficient distribution of multipartite entangled states among end users. While various architectures have been proposed, each comes with distinct advantages and limitations. Many designs depend on long-lived quantum memories and deterministic gates, which, while powerful, introduce considerable cost and technical challenges. Experimentally cheaper alternatives that circumvent these constraints are often limited to specific types of entanglement and a specific number of users. Here, we present an experiment-friendly quantum server that relies only on linear optical elements, offering a flexible approach to multipartite entanglement distribution. Our so-called photon-weaving quantum server can generate and distribute one of several locally nonequivalent graph states, including Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger (GHZ) states, as well as path, cycle, and caterpillar graph states. This is achieved through two distinct fusion protocols, i.e. multiphoton graph-state fusion (graph-state weaving) and multiphoton GHZ-state fusion (GHZ-state weaving), and can readily be implemented.

title: Parity-mixing interference in laser-assisted photoionization
authors: N Ouahioune, D Hoff, P K Maroju, C L Arnold, D Busto, A L’Huillier, M Gisselbrecht and S Carlström
abstract: Photoionization of atoms by high-order harmonics in the presence of a laser may lead to quantum interference from which information about the photoionization dynamics or the light fields can be extracted. Traditionally, this interference arises from two-photon transitions involving the absorption of consecutive harmonics combined with the absorption and stimulated emission of a laser photon. In this process, parity is conserved. Here, we investigate interference between one- and two-photon transitions in helium using high-order harmonics generated by a few-cycle laser and three-dimensional electron detection. In this case, parity is not conserved. We identify four parity-mixing interference pathways, involving two different harmonic fields or a single harmonic, together with absorption or emission of a probe photon.

title: Heralded ultrafast generation of macroscopic quantum states in matter with bright squeezed vacuum light
abstract: We show that bright squeezed vacuum light, combined with a single-shot quadrature measurement of the post-interaction light, enables the ultrafast generation of macroscopic quantum states in matter. Although in the weak-coupling regime multiphoton quantum light leaves the unconditional matter state as a classical mixture due to light–matter entanglement, quadrature-based heralding prepares the matter in a Gaussian-weighted quantum superposition of laser-driven matter states. For an ensemble of resonantly electric-dipole-coupled two-level systems, this heralding dynamics acts as a Gaussian filter with respect to the electric polarization, with brighter squeezed-vacuum light accelerating the preparation of the zero-eigenvalue Dicke state. Counter-rotating terms further drive a stroboscopic transition from this Dicke state to a cat-like state. Our results open a route to ultrafast engineering of macroscopic quantum matter with strong-field quantum light.

title: Non-Markovian quantum Mpemba effect in strongly correlated quantum dots
abstract: Harnessing non-Markovian effects has emerged as a resource for quantum control, where a structured environment can act as a quantum memory. We investigate the quench dynamics from specific initial states to equilibrium steady states in strongly correlated quantum dot systems. The distance between quantum states is quantified using the Bures metric, which endows the space of reduced density matrices with a Riemannian geometric structure. Using the numerically exact hierarchical equations of motion method, we demonstrate a quantum Mpemba effect (QME) arising from non-Markovianity. Unlike previous studies centered on non-interacting limits, we reveal a distinct non-Markovian QME uniquely driven by the initial-state-dependent formation of the many-body Kondo resonance. Furthermore, by tracking the dynamical evolution in the generalized Bloch parameter space, we uncover an intrinsic QME. This trajectory-dependent analysis provides a rigorous geometric perspective on the circuitous relaxation pathways driven by Kondo correlations. Our results underscore the critical role of memory effects in quantum quench dynamics and suggest new pathways for controlling anomalous relaxation in open quantum systems.

title: Strain-driven transition from correlated insulating to semimetallic states in twisted-bilayer graphene
authors: Lishuai Guo, Abulimiti Yasen, Mei Xiang, Wenliang Zhu and Minghu Pan
abstract: We investigate the interplay between Coulomb interaction and uniaxial heterostrain in twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) using a self-consistent Hartree–Fock (HF) approach projected onto the flat bands. For integer filling factors in the range of , we find that heterostrain strongly reconstructs the low-energy band structure and suppresses interaction-induced insulating gaps. As strain magnitude increases, the flat-band bandwidth is substantially enhanced, leading to an increased kinetic energy. The bandwidth enhancement effectively weakens the interaction strength relative to kinetic energy, resulting in the suppression of HF gaps and the emergence of semimetallic (SM) states. The strain effect can be primarily controlled by the filling factor, as well as the strain direction. At moderate strain strengths around 0.3% for , it can drive transitions between correlated insulating and SM states. In contrast, for , the HF gaps becomes negligible and the system remains essentially SM; both the strain direction and magnitude have negligible influence. Our results demonstrate that uniaxial heterostrain serves as an effective and versatile parameter for tuning correlated phases in TBG through the interplay of lattice deformation and Coulomb interactions.

title: Saturation attack of the microwave-propagated continuous variable quantum key distribution in open air
authors: Wenqi Peng, Xuan Li, Yongxin Feng, Xiu-Bo Chen and Ying Guo
abstract: Continuous variable quantum key distribution (CVQKD) can achieve the secure communication between two distant legitimate users. The microwave CVQKD exhibits stronger robustness than the optical CVQKD in transmitting quantum signals and accordingly has broad application prospects in quantum networks. Although the microwave CVQKD does not rely on the traditional optical fibers to transmit quantum signals, its practical security is still vulnerable to saturation attacks. In view of this security vulnerability, we generalize saturation attacks to microwave CVQKD and clarify the impact of saturation attacks on the parameter estimation of microwave systems. Two saturation attack schemes are further compared, one based on displacement control alone and the other on joint displacement and gain control. To mitigate the negative impacts caused by this attack, we propose a countermeasure based on the quantum nearest neighbor algorithm, which can detect saturation attacks by measuring unknown quantum states. In addition, the influence of microwave antennas on the security of the communication system is assessed, confirming that antenna gain plays a key role in determining both the secret key rate and the maximum transmission distance.

title: Phase-controlled thermal amplification in a quantum thermal transistor
abstract: We investigate phase-controlled heat transport in a quantum thermal transistor composed of three coupled two-level systems, each connected to an independent thermal reservoir. Using a nonsecular Redfield master equation, we show that a gauge-invariant phase in the triangular coupling loop provides an efficient control knob beyond reservoir temperatures: at fixed temperature bias, tuning the phase strongly modulates the steady-state heat currents and can generate pronounced thermal amplification, whereby a small variation of the control current induces large changes in the currents at the other two terminals. We further analyze how the amplification depends on the reservoir temperature as well as on the intersystem couplings, identifying regimes of enhanced performance. To clarify the underlying mechanism, we develop a complementary weak-coupling theory based on a local Lindblad equation and second-order cumulant expansion. This analysis shows that the phase first enters the exchange coherences and is then transferred to the populations through loop interference, while the heat currents are dominated by the resulting population corrections. Our results establish phase engineering as a flexible route to regulating heat flow and thermal amplification in multi-terminal quantum thermal devices.

title: Capturing an electron in the virtual state
authors: Alok Nath Singh, Bibek Bhandari, Rafael Sánchez and Andrew N Jordan
abstract: We address a foundational question in quantum mechanics: can a particle be directly found in a classically-forbidden virtual state? We instantiate this conceptual question by investigating the traversal of electrons through a tunnel barrier, which we define in a triple quantum dot system where the occupation of the central dot is energetically avoided. The motivation behind this setup is to answer whether the central dot is occupied or not during a virtual transition when it is being explicitly monitored. We investigate this problem in two different limits of continuous measurements: the stochastic quantum diffusion and the quantum jump. We find that, even though individual trajectories differ considerably across these limits, measuring leads to a higher occupation in the central dot on average. We also find that a suitably strong measurement can significantly boost the tunneling current—an effect we call measurement-assisted tunneling. Our results demonstrate that the act of observation fundamentally reshapes tunneling dynamics, resolving the seeming paradox of detecting a particle in a classically forbidden region: weak measurements partially localize the particle, while strong measurements enforce a discontinuous either/or detection or no detection outcome.
